title: Encampment eviction motion deferred; upstream equity funding reviewed
subtitle: Committee also backed affordable housing projects and a home child care parent fee cut under the national plan.
overview: At its first meeting of the new term, the Community and Health Services Committee deferred a notice of motion on encampment evictions {{vote:m1}}. The motion would have barred the Region from evicting people from the Victoria Street and Weber Street encampment in Kitchener, and from 150 Main Street in Cambridge, unless Council first passed a motion allowing it. It will return after the Superior Court issues its decision on the Region's application about the Kitchener encampment.

The committee also heard an update on reconciliation, equity, diversity and inclusion work, including the Upstream Fund. Staff reported that 41 recipients received funding. Several community groups spoke about what the funding has allowed them to do, and the committee received the report for information.

On other matters, the committee recommended funding priority projects under the P2022-19 affordable housing program {{vote:m4}}. It also recommended a parent fee reduction for the Region's licensed home child care program from January 1, 2023, as part of the national early learning and child care plan. The consent agenda was approved {{vote:m2}}. Its recommendations go to Council for a final decision.

decisions.detail: The committee deferred the notice of motion to the next committee meeting after the court decision on the Region's application is received.
The committee recommended approving the priority projects listed in the report, with Regional development charge grants and authority for staff to execute the funding agreements.
The committee recommended amending the Fees and Charges Bylaw so parent fees for children under six in the Region's licensed home child care program fall by 52.75% from January 1, 2023.
The committee received the consent agenda items for information and approved them, with no items pulled for separate discussion.

debate: Delegates from community organizations said Upstream funding helped them keep space, hire staff and plan ahead. They described past barriers such as lacking charitable status. They asked the committee to keep supporting trust-based funding.

Staff said township feedback called for more work on what upstream funding means for rural areas. They also said groups wanted funding longer than a year, so awards now run one to two years and are being reviewed for extension.

Delegates supporting the encampment motion argued that evicting people causes harm, that the new Council should be accountable for these decisions, and that a decriminalized approach to homelessness would maintain trust with people with lived experience.

One councillor said it was uncomfortable that a delegate supporting a councillor's motion was employed by that councillor, and suggested Council discuss the arrangement. The delegate said they spoke as an independent resident. Another councillor defended the delegate's long community advocacy.

A councillor noted that under the encampment policy the responsible commissioner makes eviction decisions in consultation with the CAO and Regional Solicitor, and Council is informed. The motion's mover proposed deferral and said it was not meant to interfere with the court process.
